quests.hint: 'Went' is the irregular past tense of 'go' — it doesn't end in -ed.
quests.explanation: 'Went' is one of the most common irregular past tense verbs in English. Since 'go' doesn't follow the regular -ed pattern, it simply has to be memorised.
quests.textToSpeak: We went to the beach last weekend.
quests.correctAnswer: We went to the beach last weekend.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Went' is the irregular past tense of 'go' — it doesn't end in -ed.

quests.hint: 'Bought' rhymes with 'sort' — listen closely to the vowel sound.
quests.explanation: 'Bought' is the irregular past tense of 'buy'. Notice how different it looks from the base verb — this is typical of many high-frequency irregular verbs.
quests.textToSpeak: I bought a new bag at the market.
quests.correctAnswer: I bought a new bag at the market.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Bought' rhymes with 'sort' — listen closely to the vowel sound.

quests.hint: The '-ed' in 'watched' is pronounced /t/, not /d/ or /ɪd/.
quests.explanation: Regular past tense verbs ending in a voiceless sound, like 'watch', take a /t/ sound for -ed. Getting these small sound rules right makes your speech flow more naturally.
quests.textToSpeak: They watched a film at the cinema.
quests.correctAnswer: They watched a film at the cinema.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] The '-ed' in 'watched' is pronounced /t/, not /d/ or /ɪd/.

quests.hint: 'Going to' shows a plan — say it smoothly as one phrase.
quests.explanation: 'Be going to' describes a plan or intention decided before now. It's different from 'will', which is often used for decisions made in the moment.
quests.textToSpeak: She is going to visit her cousin tomorrow.
quests.correctAnswer: She is going to visit her cousin tomorrow.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Going to' shows a plan — say it smoothly as one phrase.

quests.hint: In fast, natural speech, 'going to' often sounds like 'gonna' — but always write it in full.
quests.explanation: Native speakers often reduce 'going to' to 'gonna' in casual speech, though it's never written that way in formal English. Recognising this reduction helps your listening skills.
quests.textToSpeak: We are going to paint the fence this weekend.
quests.correctAnswer: We are going to paint the fence this weekend.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] In fast, natural speech, 'going to' often sounds like 'gonna' — but always write it in full.

quests.hint: Stress the word 'new' slightly to highlight what's changing.
quests.explanation: 'Start a new job' is a common phrase for describing a career change. 'Soon' at the end tells us the event is coming in the near future.
quests.textToSpeak: He is going to start a new job soon.
quests.correctAnswer: He is going to start a new job soon.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] Stress the word 'new' slightly to highlight what's changing.

quests.hint: 'Cheaper' adds -er for a short comparative adjective.
quests.explanation: Short adjectives like 'cheap' form comparatives with -er, while longer ones use 'more'. This is one of the first rules learners of comparison need to master.
quests.textToSpeak: This café is cheaper than the one next door.
quests.correctAnswer: This café is cheaper than the one next door.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Cheaper' adds -er for a short comparative adjective.

quests.hint: Link 'faster than' smoothly, almost as if it were a single word.
quests.explanation: 'Than' always follows a comparative adjective, connecting the two things being compared. Leaving it out is a very common mistake for learners.
quests.textToSpeak: My new phone is faster than my old one.
quests.correctAnswer: My new phone is faster than my old one.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] Link 'faster than' smoothly, almost as if it were a single word.

quests.hint: 'Much' adds extra strength before a comparative — stress it lightly.
quests.explanation: 'Much' can intensify a comparative adjective, as in 'much warmer' or 'much better'. This shows a bigger difference than the comparative alone.
quests.textToSpeak: Today is much warmer than it was yesterday.
quests.correctAnswer: Today is much warmer than it was yesterday.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Much' adds extra strength before a comparative — stress it lightly.

quests.hint: 'Couldn't' is a contraction of 'could not' — say it as one word.
quests.explanation: 'Because' introduces the reason for something. Contractions like 'couldn't' are extremely common in spoken English, so practising them builds natural fluency.
quests.textToSpeak: I couldn't sleep because the neighbours were noisy.
quests.correctAnswer: I couldn't sleep because the neighbours were noisy.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Couldn't' is a contraction of 'could not' — say it as one word.

quests.hint: 'Stayed' takes a /d/ sound for its -ed ending.
quests.explanation: Regular verbs ending in a voiced sound, like 'stay', take a /d/ sound for the past tense. This contrasts with the /t/ sound you hear after voiceless sounds.
quests.textToSpeak: She stayed home because she had a cold.
quests.correctAnswer: She stayed home because she had a cold.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Stayed' takes a /d/ sound for its -ed ending.

quests.hint: 'So' introduces the result — pause briefly before it.
quests.explanation: 'So' connects a reason to its result, while 'because' works the other way around, connecting a result to its reason. Both are essential linking words.
quests.textToSpeak: We left early so we wouldn't miss the train.
quests.correctAnswer: We left early so we wouldn't miss the train.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'So' introduces the result — pause briefly before it.

quests.hint: Use a polite, rising tone — this is a soft request, not a demand.
quests.explanation: 'Could you' is a polite way to ask for something, softer than 'Can you'. Adding 'please' makes any request sound even more courteous.
quests.textToSpeak: Could you pass me the salt, please?
quests.correctAnswer: Could you pass me the salt, please?
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] Use a polite, rising tone — this is a soft request, not a demand.

quests.hint: 'Would you mind' is followed by the -ing form of the verb.
quests.explanation: 'Would you mind' is one of the most polite ways to make a request in English. It's always followed by a verb ending in -ing, such as 'opening' or 'closing'.
quests.textToSpeak: Would you mind opening the window a little?
quests.correctAnswer: Would you mind opening the window a little?
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Would you mind' is followed by the -ing form of the verb.

quests.hint: 'Borrow' means to take something and give it back later.
quests.explanation: 'Borrow' and 'lend' are often confused: you borrow something FROM someone, and someone lends something TO you. Keeping the direction straight avoids a common mistake.
quests.textToSpeak: Can I borrow your charger for a minute?
quests.correctAnswer: Can I borrow your charger for a minute?
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Borrow' means to take something and give it back later.

quests.hint: 'Usually' goes before the main verb but after 'to be'.
quests.explanation: Adverbs of frequency like 'usually' normally sit before the main verb in a sentence. Getting the word order right is a key part of sounding natural.
quests.textToSpeak: I usually check my emails before breakfast.
quests.correctAnswer: I usually check my emails before breakfast.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Usually' goes before the main verb but after 'to be'.

quests.hint: Pause slightly before 'but' to highlight the contrast.
quests.explanation: 'But' introduces a contrast between two ideas. 'Rarely' is a negative-feeling frequency word, so it pairs naturally with a contrasting positive idea afterwards.
quests.textToSpeak: She rarely eats meat, but she loves fish.
quests.correctAnswer: She rarely eats meat, but she loves fish.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] Pause slightly before 'but' to highlight the contrast.

quests.hint: 'Hardly ever' means almost never — say both words together.
quests.explanation: 'Hardly ever' is a frequency phrase close in meaning to 'almost never'. Phrases built from two words like this are common in natural spoken English.
quests.textToSpeak: We hardly ever go out during the week.
quests.correctAnswer: We hardly ever go out during the week.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Hardly ever' means almost never — say both words together.

quests.hint: 'Downloaded' has stress on the second syllable: down-LOAD-ed.
quests.explanation: 'Download' means to transfer something from the internet to a device. Its opposite, 'upload', sends something from a device onto the internet.
quests.textToSpeak: He downloaded the app onto his new phone.
quests.correctAnswer: He downloaded the app onto his new phone.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Downloaded' has stress on the second syllable: down-LOAD-ed.

quests.hint: 'Switch off' is a phrasal verb — keep both words close together.
quests.explanation: 'Switch off' and 'turn off' both mean to stop a device from running, and they can usually be used interchangeably. Learning phrasal verb pairs like this expands your vocabulary quickly.
quests.textToSpeak: Please switch off your phone during the film.
quests.correctAnswer: Please switch off your phone during the film.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Switch off' is a phrasal verb — keep both words close together.

quests.hint: 'Froze' is irregular — it comes from 'freeze', not 'freezed'.
quests.explanation: 'Froze' here means the laptop stopped responding, a common informal use of 'freeze' for technology. Everyday tech vocabulary like this appears constantly in modern English.
quests.textToSpeak: My laptop froze in the middle of the meeting.
quests.correctAnswer: My laptop froze in the middle of the meeting.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Froze' is irregular — it comes from 'freeze', not 'freezed'.

quests.hint: 'Planning' has stress on the first syllable: PLAN-ning.
quests.explanation: 'Plan a trip' is a very common phrase for talking about future travel. Notice the doubled 'n' in 'planning', which follows a common English spelling rule.
quests.textToSpeak: We are planning a trip to the mountains.
quests.correctAnswer: We are planning a trip to the mountains.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Planning' has stress on the first syllable: PLAN-ning.

quests.hint: 'Leaves' here means 'departs', not 'leaves from a tree'.
quests.explanation: 'Leave' has several meanings in English; here it refers to a flight or vehicle departing. Context always helps you choose the correct meaning of words like this.
quests.textToSpeak: Our flight leaves early on Saturday morning.
quests.correctAnswer: Our flight leaves early on Saturday morning.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Leaves' here means 'departs', not 'leaves from a tree'.

quests.hint: 'The night before' means the previous evening — say it as one phrase.
quests.explanation: 'The night before' is a useful time expression for describing preparation. It works for any event: 'the night before the exam' or 'the night before the wedding'.
quests.textToSpeak: I packed my suitcase the night before.
quests.correctAnswer: I packed my suitcase the night before.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'The night before' means the previous evening — say it as one phrase.

quests.hint: 'The best' takes 'the' because it's a superlative.
quests.explanation: Superlative adjectives like 'best' almost always need 'the' before them. This distinguishes them from comparatives, which use 'than' instead.
quests.textToSpeak: My grandfather tells the best stories at dinner.
quests.correctAnswer: My grandfather tells the best stories at dinner.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'The best' takes 'the' because it's a superlative.

quests.hint: 'Invited' takes a soft /ɪd/ sound for its -ed ending.
quests.explanation: Verbs ending in a 't' or 'd' sound, like 'invite', add an extra /ɪd/ syllable in the past tense. This is the third and final -ed pronunciation pattern to learn.
quests.textToSpeak: Our neighbours invited us over for coffee.
quests.correctAnswer: Our neighbours invited us over for coffee.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Invited' takes a soft /ɪd/ sound for its -ed ending.

quests.hint: 'Gets along with' is a phrasal verb meaning to have a good relationship.
quests.explanation: 'Get along with someone' describes a friendly, easy relationship. 'In-laws' refers to family members gained through marriage, like a spouse's parents or siblings.
quests.textToSpeak: She gets along really well with her in-laws.
quests.correctAnswer: She gets along really well with her in-laws.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Gets along with' is a phrasal verb meaning to have a good relationship.

quests.hint: Notice two separate ideas joined by 'so' — keep a brief pause between them.
quests.explanation: This sentence links a cause and effect using 'so'. Building longer sentences from two shorter ideas is an important step in speaking more fluently.
quests.textToSpeak: The bus was late, so I missed my class.
quests.correctAnswer: The bus was late, so I missed my class.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] Notice two separate ideas joined by 'so' — keep a brief pause between them.

quests.hint: 'Anyway' at the end adds emphasis — give it a little extra stress.
quests.explanation: 'Anyway' here means 'despite that', showing the action happened even though something made it difficult. This word is useful for expressing determination.
quests.textToSpeak: I was tired, but I finished my homework anyway.
quests.correctAnswer: I was tired, but I finished my homework anyway.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Anyway' at the end adds emphasis — give it a little extra stress.

quests.hint: 'Had to' shows a strong obligation — pronounce it like 'HAD-tuh'.
quests.explanation: 'Had to' is the past form of 'must' for obligation. In fast speech, 'to' often reduces to a quick, unstressed sound, which is worth practising for natural fluency.
quests.textToSpeak: He wanted to stay, but he had to leave.
quests.correctAnswer: He wanted to stay, but he had to leave.
quests.pronunciationTips: [IPA Tip] 'Had to' shows a strong obligation — pronounce it like 'HAD-tuh'.
